questions.question: Explain why Germany was defeated in 1918.
questions.expected_answer: After Russia left the war through Brest-Litovsk, Germany moved troops west and launched the Spring Offensive on 21 March 1918 with stormtroopers, but it cost its best soldiers, outran supplies and failed by July. The Allies counter-attacked at Amiens on 8 August, the black day of the German army, and in the Hundred Days broke the Hindenburg Line, combining tanks, aircraft and artillery, while nearly two million American troops arrived. Bulgaria, the Ottoman Empire and Austria-Hungary collapsed; the blockade caused hunger; sailors mutinied at Kiel and Wilhelmshaven, revolution spread, the Kaiser abdicated on 9 November and the armistice took effect at 11 a.m. on 11 November 1918.

questions.question: Describe the aims of the Big Three at the Paris Peace Conference.
questions.expected_answer: Clemenceau of France, whose country lost about 1.4 million soldiers and suffered great destruction, wanted security, a weakened Germany and payment for damage. Lloyd George of Britain faced voters who wanted Germany punished but wanted Germany to recover for trade, feared bitterness and communism, and wanted to protect British naval and imperial power. Wilson of the United States wanted a fair, lasting peace based on the Fourteen Points: self-determination, disarmament, freedom of the seas, open diplomacy and a League of Nations. Germany could not negotiate; Botha and Smuts represented South Africa.

questions.question: Describe the main terms of the Treaty of Versailles and reactions to it.
questions.expected_answer: Signed on 28 June 1919, the treaty's Article 231 made Germany accept guilt; reparations were set in 1921 at 132 billion gold marks; the army was limited to one hundred thousand with no conscription, tanks, air force or submarines, six battleships, and a demilitarised Rhineland; Germany lost about thirteen percent of its European territory, including Alsace-Lorraine, the Saar to the League for fifteen years, the Polish Corridor and Danzig, and Anschluss was banned; colonies became mandates, with South West Africa going to South Africa; and the League of Nations was created. Germans called it a Diktat, and historians debate whether it was too harsh or too weak.
